The Law, the Principles and the Wider Map

You start with the vocabulary and rules a data protection practitioner uses every day: personal data, sensitive data, controllers and processors, and Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023. You then learn the principles and lawful bases that every later decision rests on, and see how Nigeria fits alongside other African laws and the European GDPR.
Personal data, the people involved, and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
Identify personal data and sensitive personal data in real business records

Data protection is about people, not computers. A customer list, a WhatsApp group, a register of students, a payroll sheet and a box of paper application forms all hold information about real people. When that information leaks, is misused or is kept carelessly, people can be defrauded, embarrassed, discriminated against or put in danger. This course teaches you to handle such information responsibly, and to help other organisations do the same.
What counts as personal data

**Personal data** is any information that relates to an identified or identifiable person. "Identifiable" matters: a phone number alone, a photo, a BVN, a vehicle plate number, a home address, a voice note or a customer ID that links to a name can all point to one person. If you can reasonably work out who the information is about, directly or by combining it with other information, treat it as personal data.

Some personal data is **sensitive** because misuse can cause serious harm. Nigeria's law lists categories such as genetic and biometric data (for example fingerprints used for identification), race or ethnic origin, religious or similar beliefs, health status, sex life, political opinions or affiliations, and trade union membership. Sensitive data needs a stronger reason to process it and stronger protection. Data about **children**, meaning anyone under 18 in the Act, also needs extra care, usually including the consent of a parent or guardian.

Getting the roles right tells you who carries which duties. The controller carries the main responsibility, including choosing processors that keep data safe and putting instructions to them in writing. A processor must follow the controller's instructions, keep the data secure and tell the controller quickly if something goes wrong. One organisation can be a controller for some data (its own staff records) and a processor for other data (client records it handles for someone else).
Nigeria's law in brief

The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA)** was signed into law in June 2023. It replaced the earlier regulation-based approach (the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation of 2019, issued by NITDA) with a full Act of the National Assembly, and it created the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** as the regulator. In 2025 the NDPC issued the **General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID)**, which explains in more detail how organisations should comply. Read both on the NDPC website rather than relying on summaries, because guidance is updated.
**Who it covers:** controllers and processors that are based or operating in Nigeria, processing that takes place in Nigeria, and organisations elsewhere that process the data of people in Nigeria.
**What it does not cover:** a person handling data purely for personal or household reasons, such as your own family contacts.

**Data controllers and processors of major importance:** organisations that handle a lot of personal data or data of particular value must register with the NDPC and appoint a Data Protection Officer. The GAID sets the tiers, so check the current thresholds there.

**Penalties:** the Commission can order remedies and impose fines. The maximum fine is the greater of 2% of annual gross revenue or a fixed sum (10 million naira for organisations of major importance, 2 million naira for others).
Worked example: what is the maximum fine?

For example, Halima runs a private lesson centre in Kaduna that is not of major importance. Its annual gross revenue last year was about 45 million naira. A second business, a delivery company registered as of major importance, had gross revenue of about 300 million naira.
Lesson centre: 2% of 45,000,000 = 900,000 naira. The fixed figure for a business not of major importance is 2,000,000 naira.
The law uses whichever is greater, so the ceiling is 2,000,000 naira.
Delivery company: 2% of 300,000,000 = 6,000,000 naira. Its fixed figure is 10,000,000 naira.
The greater figure is 10,000,000 naira, so that is its ceiling.
These are maximums, not automatic fines. The real lesson is that even a small business faces a ceiling far larger than the cost of a lockable cupboard, a password manager and a short staff briefing.
Why this matters beyond fines

Most harm from careless data handling falls on people. A leaked list of customer names and phone numbers feeds scam calls. Health information shared in a group chat can cost someone a job or a marriage. A photo of a child posted with a school name helps a stranger find that child. For the organisation, the cost shows up as lost trust, complaints and time spent fixing problems. Good practice is cheaper than repair.

Almost every data protection decision comes back to two questions. First, **is this processing allowed at all?** That is the lawful basis. Second, **is it being done in the right way?** That is the principles. Once you can answer both quickly, you can assess any form, app, spreadsheet or habit you meet.

The six lawful bases
The NDPA allows processing only when at least one lawful basis applies. Choose the basis **before** you collect, write it down, and tell people which one you rely on.
**Consent:** the person freely agrees to a specific use. Best when they have a real choice, such as joining a marketing list.
**Contract:** needed to deliver something the person asked for, such as an address to deliver an order.
**Legal obligation:** a law requires it, such as keeping staff pay records for tax.
**Vital interests:** needed to protect someone's life, such as giving a person's allergy information to paramedics in an emergency.
**Public interest or official authority:** mainly for government bodies and those carrying out public functions.
**Legitimate interests:** a genuine business interest that is not overridden by the person's rights, such as basic fraud checks. Weigh it honestly and record your reasoning.
What valid consent looks like

Consent is often used when another basis fits better, and it is often done badly. Under the NDPA the controller must be able to **prove** consent was given. The request must be clear, in plain language and separate from other terms. Silence, inactivity or a pre-ticked box is not consent. People can withdraw consent at any time, and withdrawing should be as easy as giving it. If saying no would cost the person a service they need, consent is not truly free, so look for another basis.

Work down the questions in order and record the first basis that genuinely fits.
Worked example: matching activities to lawful bases
For example, Chioma runs a hair salon in Port Harcourt with four stylists. She keeps a booking book, a WhatsApp Business account and a staff file.
Booking a client's appointment and calling to confirm: **contract**, because the client asked for the service.

Recording a client's scalp condition or allergy to a relaxer before treatment: this is health information, so it is **sensitive**. She needs the client's explicit consent, explained clearly, and she must keep the record locked away.
Keeping stylists' salary records: **legal obligation** for tax and pension records.
Sending promotional broadcasts about new styles: **consent**, collected with a clear opt-in question, and with "Reply STOP to leave" in every message.
Keeping CCTV at the shop entrance for security: **legitimate interests**, with a visible sign and footage kept only for a short, fixed period.
Five activities, four different bases. Chioma writes each one in her data inventory so she can explain her choices if a client or the NDPC asks.
Children's data

Where a service collects data from children, the NDPA expects the consent of a parent or legal guardian and reasonable steps to check age. Schools, tutoring centres and church youth groups should design forms for the parent to complete and sign.
Sensitive data needs a second check

For sensitive data, a normal lawful basis is not enough on its own. The NDPA allows sensitive data to be processed only in narrower situations, the most common being the person's explicit consent, a legal duty in employment, protecting someone's life, or the establishment or defence of a legal claim. In practice, ask two questions: "Do we truly need this sensitive detail?" and, if yes, "Which of the narrower conditions applies, and how will we lock this record away from everyone who does not need it?" Many organisations discover that they collect religion, ethnic group or full medical history on forms without any reason, and simply removing those fields is the safest fix.

Finally, remember that a lawful basis does not excuse breaking a principle. A school may have a good reason to collect parents' phone numbers, but it still breaks the minimisation and confidentiality principles if it then adds every parent to one large WhatsApp group where everyone can see everyone's number.
Every use of personal data needs at least one lawful basis, chosen and recorded before collection.
Consent must be clear, separate, provable and easy to withdraw; silence is never consent.
Sensitive data and children's data carry extra conditions.
A lawful basis does not excuse breaking any of the seven principles.

Data does not stay inside one country. A Lagos shop may store orders in a cloud service hosted abroad, a freelancer in Ibadan may manage a mailing list for a client in Germany, and an NGO may share beneficiary data with a donor in Kenya. To work well you need a map of the main laws and an understanding of how data can lawfully cross borders.

These laws share a common core: principles similar to the seven you learnt, lawful bases or conditions for processing, rights for individuals, security duties and a regulator. The details differ, for example in registration rules, deadlines and fines, so always read the specific law when you work in another country. At continental level, the African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (the Malabo Convention), adopted in 2014, entered into force in 2023 and encourages member states to adopt and harmonise such laws.

When the GDPR reaches a Nigerian business

The **General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)** is the European Union's law, applied since May 2018. It reaches organisations outside the EU when they offer goods or services to people in the EU, or monitor the behaviour of people in the EU. It also matters when you act as a processor for an EU client, because that client must sign a contract with you that passes on GDPR duties. GDPR fines can reach 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, and personal data breaches must usually be reported to the regulator within 72 hours.

The two laws are close cousins, so a good habit in one usually satisfies much of the other.
Cross-border transfers

Under the NDPA, sending personal data out of Nigeria, including storing it on servers abroad, is a **transfer**. It is lawful where the destination gives an adequate level of protection, or where another condition in the Act applies, such as the person's informed consent to the transfer after being told the risks, or the transfer being necessary for a contract with them. Everyday tools such as Google Drive, Gmail, Zoom and many CRM apps store data outside Nigeria, so a careful organisation lists these tools, reads their data protection terms and records why each transfer is lawful.
Worked example: a freelancer with an EU client
For example, Amaka is a virtual assistant in Enugu. A small bakery in the Netherlands hires her to manage its customer newsletter of about 1,200 subscribers.
Roles: the bakery is the controller; Amaka is a processor acting on its instructions.
Law: the bakery's customers are in the EU, so the GDPR governs the list. Amaka should expect a written data processing agreement and should read it before signing.
Security: she turns on two-step verification on the email platform, uses a password manager, and never downloads the full list to her personal phone.
Scope: she uses the list only for the newsletter, not for her own marketing.
Incident plan: the agreement says she must tell the bakery quickly if she suspects a breach, so she saves the bakery owner's contact details and the steps in a note.
Amaka wins trust by asking for the processing agreement herself. Her careful setup becomes a selling point for future international clients.
Where these skills are used
**Data Protection Officer (DPO):** required for organisations of major importance under the NDPA, and often an in-house role in banks, fintechs, telecoms, hospitals and schools.
**Data Protection Compliance Organisations (DPCOs):** firms licensed by the NDPC to provide audits, training and compliance services. They hire analysts and trainers.
**Built into other roles:** HR officers, marketers, virtual assistants, software developers and NGO programme staff all handle personal data and are more valuable when they handle it well.
**Recognised learning paths:** international certifications such as the IAPP's CIPP/E and CIPM, plus NDPC publications and training.

A practical way to build your knowledge is to keep a one-page "law card" for each country you work with: the name of the law, the regulator's website, the lawful bases or conditions, the breach reporting rule, any registration duty and the rules on sending data abroad. Fill each card only from the official text or the regulator's own guidance, write the date you checked it, and refresh it every six months. When a client from Kenya or South Africa calls, you can then speak with confidence and show exactly where each point comes from.
Start with your own country's text
When a client asks "which law applies", start with where they operate and where the people in their data live. Then read that law's official text or regulator guidance, not a blog summary.

How to collect the information

Worked example: one small NGO, one sheet
For example, Bisi coordinates a women's savings and skills NGO in Ibadan with three staff and about 260 members. She builds her first inventory in Google Sheets in one afternoon.
She lists five data categories: member registration, savings records, training attendance, staff files and donor contacts.
Tracing member registration, she finds the data in three places: paper forms in a cupboard, a Google Sheet, and photos of the forms on a staff member's phone.
The phone photos have no purpose once the sheet is updated, so she has them deleted and asks staff to type directly into the sheet in future.
The registration form asks for religion and tribe. No activity uses either, so she removes both fields from the next print run.
The Google Sheet was shared as "anyone with the link can view". She changes it to the three named staff only.
One afternoon of mapping removed two unnecessary sensitive fields, a full set of uncontrolled copies and an open link. These fixes cost nothing.
Locking down the tools you already use
**Google Drive and Sheets:** share with named people, not "anyone with the link"; give "Viewer" unless editing is needed; review sharing every quarter using the share settings on each file.

**Google or Microsoft accounts:** turn on two-step verification for every account that can open personal data, and use a business account rather than a personal one so access can be removed when someone leaves.

**WhatsApp Business:** turn on two-step verification, limit who can add the number to groups, and avoid broadcasting to groups where members can see each other's numbers. Use broadcast lists, which only reach contacts who saved your number.
**Phones and laptops:** use a screen lock, keep software updated, and turn on device encryption and remote wipe where available.
**Paper:** a lockable cupboard, a clear-desk habit and shredding of forms that are no longer needed.

Controlling who can see what

The principle behind access control is **need to know**: each person gets access only to the data their job requires, and loses it when the job changes. In practice, keep a short access list for each important file or system, naming who has access and why. When a staff member leaves, remove their access on their last day, change any shared passwords they knew, and collect any devices. Avoid shared logins such as one password for "office@" used by five people, because you cannot tell who did what. Give each person their own account wherever the tool allows it.
Keep the inventory itself safe

The inventory describes where sensitive data lives, which makes it useful to an attacker. Share it only with the people who maintain it, and do not paste real personal data into it, only descriptions.

With an inventory in hand, the next step is a **gap assessment**: a structured comparison between what the organisation does now and what good practice and the law expect. The output is a ranked list of problems and fixes, so that limited time and money go to the biggest risks first.
Step one: test each principle

Take each row of the inventory and ask the quick test question for each principle from Module 1. Record every "no" or "not sure" as a gap, with a short description and the evidence you saw. Be specific: "Member sheet shared with anyone with the link" is useful, while "weak security" is not.
Step two: score each gap

A simple and widely used approach scores each risk for **likelihood** (how probable it is that harm happens) and **impact** (how bad the harm would be for the people affected), each from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). Multiply them to get a score from 1 to 25. Scores of 15 or more are high and need action now, 8 to 14 are medium and need a planned fix, and 7 or below are low and can be monitored. Agree the scale with the client before you start, and write down the reason for each score so others can check it.
Likelihood and impact grid
Low likelihood, high impact: plan safeguards
High likelihood, high impact: act now
Low likelihood, low impact: monitor
High likelihood, low impact: quick fixes
Likelihood of harm
Impact on people
Place each gap in a quadrant to see at a glance which ones need action first.
Worked example: ranking four gaps
For example, Tunde is assessing a private clinic in Abuja with 11 staff. Patient records are on paper and in a shared spreadsheet.
Gap A: the patient spreadsheet, which includes diagnoses, is open to all 11 staff, including two part-time front desk volunteers. Likelihood 4, impact 5, score 20: high.
Gap B: no written retention period for old records. Likelihood 3, impact 3, score 9: medium.
Gap C: the reception computer has no screen lock and faces the waiting area. Likelihood 4, impact 4, score 16: high.
Gap D: the privacy notice on the wall is out of date. Likelihood 2, impact 2, score 4: low.
Ranking: A (20), C (16), B (9), D (4). He proposes fixing A and C within one week, B within two months, and D at the next reprint.
The clinic's owner sees a short, reasoned list instead of a long list of worries, and agrees to restrict the spreadsheet to the doctors and two nurses that same day.

When a Data Privacy Impact Assessment is required

The NDPA requires a **Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA)** before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights and freedoms. A DPIA is a deeper version of the same thinking, done for one planned activity before it starts. Typical triggers include large-scale processing of sensitive data, new technology such as fingerprint or face recognition, systematic monitoring of people, and combining data sets in ways people would not expect. Check the GAID and NDPC guidance for the current list and any template.
**Describe the processing:** what data, whose, why, how, where it goes, and for how long.
**Check necessity and proportion:** is there a less intrusive way to achieve the purpose?
**Identify and score risks** to the people affected, not only to the organisation.
**List the safeguards** that reduce each risk, and the score after safeguards.
**Decide and sign off:** go ahead, change the plan, or stop. If high risk remains, consult the NDPC before starting.
**Review** the DPIA when the activity changes.
Biometric attendance is a common trigger

Schools and companies increasingly use fingerprint clock-in machines. Fingerprints used to identify people are biometric data, a sensitive category, so this is a classic case for a DPIA and for asking whether a card or PIN would do the job.

A short DPIA can fit on two or three pages. What matters is that it is honest, done before the activity starts, signed by someone with authority, and kept with the inventory. If the organisation has a Data Protection Officer, the DPO should be consulted and their advice recorded, even when management decides differently.
Step three: the action plan

Turn the ranked gaps into an action plan with four columns: the fix, the owner, the deadline and how you will know it is done. Keep fixes concrete, such as "Change spreadsheet sharing to named doctors and nurses; owner: practice manager; by Friday; evidence: screenshot of sharing settings". A plan that names owners and evidence gets done; a plan full of general advice does not. Review progress with the client after 30 days and update the scores.

Good data protection is mostly routine: answering people who ask about their data, deleting what is no longer needed, and knowing exactly what to do when something goes wrong. These three routines are where many organisations fail, and where a practitioner adds clear value.
Data subject rights

Under the NDPA, people can ask to be told about and get a copy of their data, to have it corrected, to have it deleted in many situations, to restrict its use, to withdraw consent, to object to processing including direct marketing, not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them, and in some cases to receive their data in a portable format. A request does not need special words. "Please remove me from your list" on WhatsApp is a valid request.
Log the request the day it arrives: date, person, channel and what they asked for.
Confirm identity in a proportionate way, for example by replying to the phone number or email already on file, so you do not hand data to an impostor.
Search every location in the inventory for that person's data.
Act on the request or explain clearly, in writing, any part you cannot do and why (for example records you must keep by law).
Reply in plain language, record the date you closed the request, and keep the log.
Set an internal target such as 14 days, and check the GAID for the legal deadline that applies.
A person moving files into a bin
Deleting data on time is a protection, not a loss.
Retention schedules

Storage limitation means each data category needs a retention period and a trigger for deletion. Base the period on the purpose and on any law that requires records to be kept, such as tax or employment rules, and write down the reason. Then make deletion happen: put review dates in a calendar, and use secure methods such as shredding paper and deleting files from both the folder and the trash.

When something goes wrong

A **personal data breach** is any security incident that leads to personal data being lost, destroyed, changed, disclosed or accessed without permission. It includes a stolen phone with customer chats, a spreadsheet sent to the wrong WhatsApp group, a hacked email account and a box of forms left in a taxi. Under the NDPA, where a breach is likely to put people's rights and freedoms at risk, the controller must notify the NDPC within **72 hours** of becoming aware of it. Where the risk to people is high, the controller must also tell the affected people immediately, in plain language, with advice on how to protect themselves. A processor must tell the controller without undue delay.
The first 72 hours of a breach
Hour 0: become aware, log it
Hours 0 to 4: contain the damage
Hours 4 to 24: assess risk
Before hour 72: notify NDPC if risk
Immediately if high risk: tell people
The clock starts when the organisation becomes aware, not when the investigation ends.
Worked example: a lost phone with customer chats

For example, Ngozi runs an online fabric store in Onitsha. At 9:00 am on Monday her sales assistant reports that the shop's WhatsApp Business phone was stolen on the bus the evening before. The phone holds chats with about 400 customers, including addresses and payment screenshots.
Awareness: Ngozi learns of it at 9:00 am Monday, so 72 hours later is 9:00 am Thursday. She writes this deadline at the top of her breach log.

Containment by 10:00 am: she has the SIM blocked with the network provider, uses Google's Find My Device to lock and erase the phone, and collects a replacement SIM and registers WhatsApp on a new phone with the same number, which logs the stolen phone out.

Assessment by Monday evening: names, phone numbers, addresses and payment screenshots of about 400 people could be exposed. Fraudsters could use them for convincing scam calls, so she judges the risk as real and likely high.
Notification on Tuesday: she reports to the NDPC through the channel shown on its website, describing what happened, the data and people involved, the likely consequences and the steps taken.
Telling customers on Tuesday: a short broadcast explains the theft, warns that the shop will never ask for a PIN or OTP, and gives the official number to check any call.
Ngozi notifies about 24 hours inside the deadline and her customers hear the news from her first. Afterwards she adds a screen lock rule and stops saving payment screenshots on the phone.
Keep a breach log even for small incidents

Record every incident, even ones you decide not to report: what happened, when you found out, the data involved, your risk decision and reasons, and the fixes. This log shows accountability and helps you spot patterns, such as repeated wrong-recipient emails.
Rights requests can arrive in any words on any channel; log, verify, search, act, reply.
Every data category needs a retention period, a reason and a deletion habit.
Report risky breaches to the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware, and tell people immediately if the risk is high.
Contain first, then assess, notify and learn.

Advising Clients, Writing Policies and Leading Change

In the final module you work as an adviser. You run a discovery interview, write a privacy notice that ordinary people can understand, scope and price a data protection engagement honestly, and build a portfolio and staff-training habit that make you trusted inside an organisation or as an independent practitioner.
Running a discovery interview and site walk-through
Prepare a discovery question set grouped by topic
Run an interview that uncovers real practice, not just stated policy
Observe and record evidence during a walk-through without collecting personal data yourself

Every engagement starts with discovery: understanding how an organisation really handles personal data before you advise. Generic advice fails because every business is different. A bakery, a church and a fintech start-up all hold personal data, but in very different amounts, types and places. Good discovery gives you the facts for the inventory and the gap assessment, and it builds the client's trust.
Prepare: the question set
Topic
Example questions
People and data
Whose personal data do you hold: customers, staff, students, members, donors? Roughly how many people?
Collection
Where does data come in: forms, WhatsApp, website, walk-ins, referrals? Can I see each form?
What do you use each item for? Is anything collected but never used?
Storage and access
Where is it kept, on paper and online? Who can open it? What happens when someone leaves?
Sharing
Which apps, partners, banks or donors receive personal data? Is there a written agreement?
When do you delete anything? Who decides?
Incidents
Has anything ever been lost, stolen, hacked or sent to the wrong person? What happened next?
Regulation
Have you registered with the NDPC, appointed a DPO or filed any compliance returns? Has anyone checked whether you are of major importance?
Two people talking across a table with notes
Discovery is a conversation: ask, listen, then ask to see the evidence.
Interview technique
**Interview the people who do the work,** not only the owner. The receptionist knows where the forms really go.
**Ask for examples:** "Show me the last form you filled" reveals more than "Do you collect data responsibly?"
**Use open, non-judgemental questions.** People hide practices they fear will get them blamed. Explain that you are looking for fixes, not culprits.
**Note the difference between policy and practice.** A written policy that says "files are locked" means little if the cupboard key hangs on the door.
**Confirm your understanding** at the end by reading back your main points.
The walk-through

After the interview, ask to walk through the places where data lives: reception, offices, the store room, shared computers. Look for screens visible to visitors, unlocked cabinets, documents on desks, passwords on sticky notes, old computers waiting for disposal and printers holding forgotten pages. Take notes and, with permission, photos of **settings and locations only**, never of documents showing someone's personal data. You should leave with evidence of the problem, not a copy of it.
Worked example: discovery at a nursery and primary school
For example, Funmi is invited to review a private nursery and primary school in Lekki with about 180 pupils and 22 staff.
Before the visit she sends her question set to the proprietor and asks for blank copies of the admission form, the staff application form and the photo consent form.

In the interview the proprietor says photos are only used with consent. The admin officer later shows her that the admission form has one line: "I agree to all school policies", with no separate photo consent.

On the walk-through she notes that pupils' medical forms, which list allergies and conditions, sit in an open tray in the staff room, and the school's Facebook page shows pupils in uniform with full names in the captions.
She asks how many parents are in the class WhatsApp groups and learns that each group shows every parent's number to every other parent.
She writes a one-page discovery note with eight findings, each linked to a principle, and marks three as urgent: medical forms, photo consent and names on public posts.
The school receives a clear note within two days. Because Funmi showed the gap between what was said and what happens, the proprietor asks her to proceed to a full gap assessment.
Writing the discovery note

Keep the note to one page so the client actually reads it. Start with two sentences on what you looked at and when. Then list each finding in the same pattern: what you saw, which principle it affects, and why it matters to the people whose data it is. End with the three most urgent items and the proposed next step. Avoid blame and avoid jargon: "Medical forms are kept in an open tray in the staff room, where visitors and all staff can read them" is clearer and fairer than "serious integrity and confidentiality failure". Send it within a few days, while the visit is fresh for everyone.
Discovery in five moves
Send questions ahead
Interview owner and staff
Walk through workspaces
Check forms and tools
Write one-page discovery note
Each move tests the one before it, so stated policy is checked against real practice.
Protect what you learn

As an adviser you will see confidential information. Sign a confidentiality agreement, keep your notes free of personal data where possible, store them securely and delete them at the end of the engagement as agreed. You are a processor or a trusted third party, so your own habits are part of the client's risk.
Discovery finds real practice by interviewing the people who do the work and asking for examples.

Writing a plain-language privacy notice and scoping a paid engagement

Transparency is one of the seven principles, and the privacy notice is its main tool. A notice copied from a big company's website and pasted into a small business's page usually describes processing that does not happen and misses what does. A good notice is written from the inventory, so it is true, specific and short.
What a privacy notice should cover
Who you are and how to contact you, including the DPO if you have one.
What personal data you collect and where it comes from.
Why you use it and the lawful basis for each purpose.
Who you share it with, including processors, and whether it goes outside Nigeria.
How long you keep it.
How you protect it, in general terms.
The person's rights and exactly how to use them, including how to complain to the NDPC.
The date of the notice and how you will tell people about changes.
Plain language techniques

Write as you would speak to a respected customer. Use "we" and "you". Keep sentences short and put the most important information first. Replace legal phrases with ordinary ones: "we keep" instead of "we retain", "we share with" instead of "we may disclose to third parties". Use headings that are questions, such as "What do we collect?" and "How long do we keep it?". Consider a short version for a poster or WhatsApp catalogue, with a link to the full notice. Where many customers prefer Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or Pidgin, a faithful translation of the short version builds real understanding.
A person filling in a form on a large screen
A clear notice next to the form tells people what will happen to what they write.
Instead of this
Write this
We may process your personal data for legitimate business purposes
We use your phone number to confirm and deliver your order
Data may be disclosed to third parties
We share your name, phone and address with the delivery company we use, only to deliver your order
Data will be retained as long as necessary
We delete your delivery details 12 months after your last order
Data subjects may exercise their rights
To see, correct or delete your details, send "MY DATA" to our WhatsApp number and we will reply within 14 days
Test it on real readers

Give the draft to three people who are like the organisation's customers. Ask them to tell you, in their own words, what data is collected, why, and how to ask for deletion. Wherever they hesitate, rewrite.
Scoping the engagement
Clients often say "make us compliant", which is not a scope. Offer clear tiers so the client can choose, and write down what is included and what is not.
Engagement tiers from base to top
Ongoing support retainer
Policies, notices and training
Gap assessment and action plan
Discovery and data inventory
Each tier builds on the one below, so an inventory always comes first.

Be clear about two limits. First, you are giving practical compliance support, not legal opinions; refer questions of legal interpretation or disputes to a lawyer. Second, under NDPC rules, some formal compliance services, such as audits whose results are filed with the Commission for organisations of major importance, are provided through licensed Data Protection Compliance Organisations. If you are not licensed, describe your work as a readiness review and help the client prepare for, or work alongside, a licensed DPCO.
Worked example: pricing a school engagement

For example, Funmi prices the next stage for the Lekki school from Lesson 1. Her rate, based on her experience and local rates for similar professional work, is about 10,000 naira per hour (approximate, for illustration only).

She estimates the hours: data inventory 6, gap assessment and action plan 6, privacy notice and photo consent form 5, staff training session including preparation 4, review meeting 2. Total = 6 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 23 hours.
Base fee: 23 x 10,000 = 230,000 naira.
She adds 15% for unexpected extra work: 230,000 x 0.15 = 34,500 naira. Total = 264,500 naira, which she rounds to 265,000 naira.
Payment terms: 50% on signing (132,500 naira) and 50% on delivery (132,500 naira).
Out of scope, listed in writing: legal opinions, NDPC registration filing, changes to the school's software, and any work beyond one training session.
The proprietor sees exactly what 265,000 naira buys and what it does not. Two months later the school adds a quarterly review retainer, priced separately.

Explain value, not only hours. A clean inventory, a true notice and trained staff reduce the chance of a costly incident, protect the reputation that brings in clients, and prepare the organisation for questions from partners, banks and donors who increasingly ask about data protection.

Policies do not protect data; people do. Most incidents in small organisations come from everyday actions: a list sent to the wrong group, a phone without a screen lock, a stranger allowed to read a file. Leading change means helping staff build a few habits that stick, and showing your own competence in a way others can trust.
A 30-minute staff briefing
Minutes
Segment
What you do
0 to 5
Why it matters here
Tell a short, true-to-life story from this organisation's world, for example a parent upset that their child's photo was posted
5 to 15
Five house rules
Lock screens, share files with named people only, never forward lists to groups, shred forms, report incidents immediately
Practice
Small groups decide what to do in three short scenarios
Who to call
Name the person to report incidents to and how; hand out a one-page summary
A presenter explaining a chart to colleagues
A short, practical briefing changes daily habits more than a long policy document.

Make reporting safe. If staff fear punishment, they hide mistakes, and a hidden breach cannot be contained or reported within 72 hours. Thank people who report quickly, and focus on fixing the process. Repeat the briefing for new staff and refresh it once a year.
Writing good scenarios

Scenarios work best when they come from the organisation's real work and have one clearly better answer. For a pharmacy, for example: "A caller says she is a customer's sister and asks what medicine he collected last week. What do you do?" The right answer is to share nothing and offer to pass a message to the customer, because health information is sensitive and the caller's identity is unknown. For a school: "A parent asks you to send the class list so she can invite everyone to a birthday party." The better answer is to offer to pass her invitation to parents, not to send their numbers. Discuss why the answer is right, not just what it is, so staff can handle situations you did not predict.
Leading from inside an organisation

You do not need the title of Data Protection Officer to lead. Volunteer to build the inventory for your team, suggest a quarterly ten-minute check of who has access to shared files, and offer to review new forms before they are printed. Bring problems to managers with a fix and an estimate of effort, not just a warning. Over time, people start asking for your view before they launch a new form, app or campaign, which is exactly where data protection should begin.
Your portfolio

**A case study:** the inventory, gap assessment and action plan for a real organisation (with written permission and all identifying details removed) or a well-researched fictional one, clearly labelled.
**A privacy notice and a consent form** you drafted, with before and after versions if you improved an existing one.
**A DPIA** for a realistic high-risk activity, such as biometric attendance.
**A training pack:** your briefing outline, scenarios and one-page summary.
**Evidence of results,** such as a short client statement about what changed, shared with permission.
Worked example: turning one project into three portfolio pieces
For example, Zainab completed a readiness review for a fashion retailer in Kano as a volunteer. The owner agreed she could use the work if the business was not named.
She replaces the business name with "a fashion retailer in northern Nigeria" and removes every customer and staff detail.
Piece 1: a two-page case study showing the 12 gaps she found, their scores, and the 5 fixed within 30 days.
Piece 2: the before and after privacy notice, showing the reading improvements she made.
Piece 3: her staff briefing slides and the three scenarios she wrote.
She adds the owner's two-sentence statement and saves everything as one PDF and a LinkedIn Featured post.
One volunteer project gives Zainab a credible portfolio. In conversations with prospective clients she can show real work while proving she respects confidentiality.

Follow the NDPC's website for the Act, the GAID and new guidance, and re-read them before each engagement. If you want an international credential, the IAPP's certifications such as CIPP/E (European law) and CIPM (running a privacy programme) are widely recognised; check current fees and exam formats on the IAPP website before committing. Join professional communities, follow announcements from regulators in the countries you serve, and pair this course with cybersecurity learning so your security advice stays current.

Personal data: anything that can identify a person
Sensitive data: health, religion, biometrics and more
Children under 18 need extra care
Data protection is about people, not computers.
A customer list, a WhatsApp group, a register of students, a payroll sheet and a box of paper forms all hold information about real people.
Personal data is any information that can point to one person. A phone number, a photo, a BVN, a home address or a voice note can all do it, alone or combined with other details.

Some data is sensitive, because misuse can cause serious harm. Health, religious beliefs, ethnic origin, political opinions and fingerprints are examples. Sensitive data needs a stronger reason and stronger protection.
Data about children, meaning anyone under 18 in the Act, also needs extra care, usually with a parent or guardian's consent.
Name the roles first
The three people involved
The person the data is about. For example, a customer who orders a gown from a tailor.
Decides why and how data is used. The tailoring business that keeps measurements and phone numbers.
Handles data for the controller, on its instructions. A bookkeeper or a cloud app the tailor uses.
Before you decide who must do what, name the three roles correctly. The data subject is the person the data is about, like a customer who orders a gown.
The data controller decides why and how the data is used. Here, the tailoring business. The controller carries the main responsibility.
The data processor handles the data on the controller's behalf, such as a bookkeeper or a cloud app. A processor must follow instructions, keep data secure and report problems quickly.
The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
Signed into law in June 2023
Regulator: the NDPC
Detailed guidance: the GAID, issued in 2025
Covers anyone processing data of people in Nigeria
Not for purely personal or household use
The NDPA was signed into law in June 2023.
It created the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, the NDPC, as the regulator.
In 2025 the NDPC issued the GAID, which explains in more detail how to comply. Read both on the NDPC website.
The Act covers organisations based or operating in Nigeria, and organisations elsewhere that process the data of people in Nigeria.
It does not cover you handling your own family contacts for purely personal reasons.
Worked example
Halima's maximum fine
For example, Halima's lesson centre in Kaduna, not of major importance, earned about 45 million naira.
2% of annual gross revenue
Fixed sum for her tier
These are maximums, not automatic fines.
The NDPC can impose fines. The maximum is the greater of 2% of annual gross revenue, or a fixed sum. Let us work it out for Halima's lesson centre in Kaduna.
Her revenue last year was about 45 million naira. 2% of that is 900,000 naira.
The fixed figure for a business not of major importance is 2,000,000 naira. For organisations of major importance it is 10,000,000 naira.
The law uses whichever is greater, so her ceiling is 2,000,000 naira.
That is far more than the cost of a lockable cupboard, a password manager and a short staff briefing.
Step by step
A lawful basis never excuses breaking a principle.
Is it needed for their contract?
Otherwise, ask clear consent
Every use of personal data needs a lawful basis, chosen and written down before you collect. Work down these questions in order.
First, define the exact purpose in one sentence.
Does a law require it? Keeping staff pay records for tax is a legal obligation.
Is it needed to deliver what the person asked for? A delivery address for an order is contract.
Is there a genuine business interest that does not override the person's rights, like basic fraud checks? That is legitimate interests. Record your reasoning.
If none of these fits, ask for clear consent, for example to join a marketing list.
And remember the principles, such as collecting only what you need. A school with a good reason to collect parents' numbers still breaks the rules if it puts every parent in one big WhatsApp group.
Common mistake
Is this consent valid?
Valid consent
Clear, plain language
Separate from other terms
You can prove it was given
Easy to withdraw
Not consent
Silence or doing nothing
A pre-ticked box
Saying no costs a needed service
Hidden inside other terms

Consent is often used when another basis fits better, and it is often done badly. Valid consent is clear, in plain language, separate from other terms, and provable. Withdrawing should be as easy as giving it.
Silence, inactivity or a pre-ticked box is never consent. And if saying no would cost the person a service they need, consent is not truly free, so look for another basis.
Key points
Remember
Personal data is anything that can identify a person
Name subject, controller and processor first
NDPA 2023 is enforced by the NDPC
Choose and record a lawful basis before collecting
Data on servers abroad is a transfer
To remember. Personal data is anything that can identify a person. Name the three roles first. The NDPA is enforced by the NDPC.
Choose and record a lawful basis before you collect. And storing data on servers abroad is a transfer, which needs a lawful condition too.

Why this matters
You cannot protect what you have not found
A data inventory lists all personal data you hold
Why, where, who can see it, how long it is kept
The first document an auditor asks for
Most early fixes cost nothing
This module turns the law into working tools. It starts with one simple table, the data inventory, also called a data map.
It lists each type of personal data an organisation holds, why it holds it, where it is stored, who can see it and how long it is kept.
It is the first document a data protection auditor asks for, and the base for everything else.
And the good news: most of the first fixes you find will cost nothing.
Step by step
Building your data inventory
Start from every form and channel
Follow each data type after it arrives
Walk around and look: cupboards, phones
Ask staff: where else might this be?
Write it down and mark the gaps
Step one. Start from every place data comes in: paper forms, website forms, WhatsApp numbers, email addresses and apps.
Step two. Follow each type of data after it arrives. Who copies it, where is it saved, who is it forwarded to?
Step three. Walk around and look. Filing cabinets, notebooks, phone galleries, laptops and flash drives.
Step four. Ask staff where else the data might be. People often keep private copies to make their work easier.
Step five. Write each finding into the sheet and mark anything unnecessary or unprotected.

For example, Bisi did this for her NGO in Ibadan in one afternoon. She found photos of member forms on a staff phone, religion and tribe fields nobody used, and a sheet open to anyone with the link. She fixed all three at no cost.
Free protections
Lock down the tools you already use
Drive: share with named people, not the link
Two-step verification on every account
WhatsApp: broadcast lists, not open groups
Phones: screen lock, updates, remote wipe
Paper: locked cupboard, shred old forms
In Google Drive, share with named people, not anyone with the link, and give view only unless editing is needed.
Turn on two-step verification for every account that can open personal data.
On WhatsApp Business, use broadcast lists instead of groups where members can see each other's numbers.
Phones and laptops need a screen lock, updated software and remote wipe where available.
Paper needs a lockable cupboard and shredding. And when someone leaves, remove their access on their last day.
Score each gap
Likelihood times impact
Act now. Tunde's clinic: patient sheet with diagnoses open to all 11 staff. 4 times 5 is 20.
Plan a fix. No written retention period for old records. 3 times 3 is 9.
Monitor. An out-of-date privacy notice on the wall. 2 times 2 is 4.
Next, compare what the organisation does with each principle, and score every gap. Likelihood of harm from 1 to 5, times impact on people from 1 to 5, gives a score from 1 to 25.
15 or more is high. For example, Tunde assessed a clinic in Abuja where the patient spreadsheet, with diagnoses, was open to all 11 staff. Likelihood 4, impact 5, score 20. Act now.
8 to 14 is medium and needs a planned fix, like having no retention period, which scored 9.
7 or below is low and can be monitored. Write the reason for each score, then give every fix an owner, a deadline and evidence it is done.
When it goes wrong
The clock starts when you become aware, not when you finish.
Hours 4 to 24: assess the risk
Before hour 72: notify the NDPC if risky
High risk: tell affected people at once
A breach is any incident where personal data is lost, changed, disclosed or accessed without permission. A stolen phone, a list sent to the wrong group, a hacked email. Log it the moment you know.
Contain the damage first. For example, when Ngozi's shop phone with chats from about 400 customers was stolen, she blocked the SIM, erased the phone remotely and moved WhatsApp to a new phone.
Then assess the risk. Her customers' names, addresses and payment screenshots could feed scam calls, so the risk was real.
Where a breach is likely to put people at risk, notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware.
If the risk is high, tell the people affected immediately, in plain language. Ngozi warned customers that the shop will never ask for a PIN or OTP.
Rights requests
When someone asks about their data
Log it the day it arrives
Confirm identity using details on file
Search every place in the inventory
Act, or explain in writing what you cannot do
Reply plainly and close the log
People can ask for a copy of their data, to correct it, or to delete it. A request needs no special words. Please remove me from your list, sent on WhatsApp, is valid.
Log it, confirm who they are, search every location, act or explain what you cannot do, and reply plainly.
Key points
Remember
Trace every copy: phones, paper, email
Delete stray copies and unneeded fields
Score gaps: likelihood times impact
Each data type needs a retention period
Contain, assess, notify within 72 hours
To remember. Trace every copy. Delete what you do not need. Score gaps and fix the highest first.
Give each type of data a retention period. And in a breach, contain first, then assess and notify within 72 hours.

Working as an adviser
Find real practice, not stated policy
Every business holds data differently
Interview the people who do the work
Ask to see the last form they filled
Look for fixes, not culprits
Generic advice fails, because a bakery, a church and a fintech all hold personal data in very different ways. So every engagement starts with discovery.
Interview the people who do the work, not only the owner. The receptionist knows where the forms really go.
Ask for examples. Show me the last form you filled tells you more than asking if they collect data responsibly.
And explain that you are looking for fixes, not culprits. People hide practices they fear will get them blamed.
Step by step
Photograph settings and places, never someone's personal data.
Send your questions ahead
Interview the owner and staff
Walk through the workspaces
Check the forms and tools
Write a one-page discovery note
Step one. Send your question set ahead and ask for blank copies of the forms.

Step two. Interview the owner and the staff. For example, Funmi reviewed a school in Lekki. The proprietor said photos were only used with consent, but the admission form just said, I agree to all school policies.
Step three. Walk through reception, offices and the staff room. Funmi found pupils' medical forms, listing allergies, in an open tray.
Take notes, and with permission, photos of settings and locations only. Leave with evidence of the problem, not a copy of it.
Step four. Check the forms and tools, such as class WhatsApp groups that show every parent's number to every other parent.
Step five. Write a one-page note. For each finding, say what you saw, which principle it affects, and why it matters. End with the three most urgent items.
The privacy notice
Write it the way you speak
Disclosed to third parties
Retained as long as necessary
Data subjects may exercise rights
We share it with our delivery company
We delete it 12 months after your order
Send MY DATA to our WhatsApp
A privacy notice copied from a big company's website describes things that do not happen and misses what does. Write it from your inventory, so it is true and short. Avoid legal phrases like these.
Use we and you, and short sentences. We share your name and address with the delivery company, only to deliver your order. We delete your details 12 months after your last order.
Then test it on three people like the customers. Wherever they hesitate, rewrite.
Pricing the work
Funmi prices the school engagement
For example, Funmi charges about 10,000 naira per hour and estimates 23 hours of work.
Base fee: 23 hours
Add 15% for unexpected work
Approximate, for illustration only.
Clients often say make us compliant, which is not a scope. Offer clear tiers, list what is not included, and price from hours.
Funmi adds up inventory, gap assessment, notice, training and a review meeting. That is 23 hours, at about 10,000 naira, so 230,000 naira.
She adds 15% for unexpected extra work, which is 34,500 naira.
That makes 264,500 naira, which she rounds to 265,000 naira, with 50% on signing and 50% on delivery.
In writing, she excludes legal opinions and NDPC registration filing. You give practical support, not legal opinions.
Leading change
0 to 5: a true-to-life story
5 to 15: five house rules
15 to 25: practise three scenarios
25 to 30: who to call, one-page summary
Policies do not protect data. People do. Start with a short story from their world, like a parent upset that a child's photo was posted.
Then teach five house rules.
Practise real scenarios. For a pharmacy: a caller says she is a customer's sister and asks what medicine he collected. The right answer is to share nothing and offer to pass a message.
End by naming who to report incidents to, and hand out a one-page summary.
House rules
Five habits for every staff member
Lock your screen
Share files with named people only
Never forward lists to groups
Shred forms you no longer need
Report incidents immediately
Lock screens. Share with named people only. Never forward lists to groups. Shred old forms. Report incidents immediately.
And make reporting safe. If staff fear punishment, they hide mistakes, and a hidden breach cannot be reported within 72 hours.
Key points
Remember
Check stated policy against real practice
Write notices from the inventory, in plain words
Scope in tiers and list exclusions
Make incident reporting safe
Build a portfolio with personal data removed
To remember. Check what people say against what really happens. Write notices in plain words. Scope in tiers and list exclusions. Make reporting safe.
And build your portfolio from real or clearly labelled work, with every personal detail removed.
